# Deuteronomy 18 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter falls into two main sections: **vv. 1–8**, provision for priests and Levites, and **vv. 9–22**, prescriptions for prophets — first a prohibition of occult practices (vv. 9–14), then the promise of a Prophet like Moses and tests for true and false prophets (vv. 15–22). Matthew Henry notes that after the offices of judge and king (chapters 16–17), Deuteronomy now turns to priest and prophet. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/deuteronomy/18.htm)

---

## vv. 1–2 — The Inheritance of the Levites

**v. 1:** “The Levitical priests—indeed the whole tribe of Levi—shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel. They are to eat the offerings made by fire to the LORD; that is their inheritance.”

The tribe of Levi received no territorial allotment in Canaan. David Guzik (Enduring Word) explains they were instead distributed throughout the land (Joshua 21) and supported by the gifts and offerings of God’s people — they received at least a portion of most sacrificial animals (Numbers 18:8–9). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

The Pulpit Commentary clarifies that “the offerings of the Lord made by fire” here refers specifically to the meal offering, sin offering, and trespass offering (cf. Numbers 18:9). “And His inheritance” means what was appropriated to Jehovah and from Him to the tribe of Levi — tithes, firstlings, and firstfruits. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-18.html)

Precept Austin notes that only descendants of Aaron were called “priests”; the rest of Levi (Gershonites and Merarites) assisted the priests. The Levites who did not serve at the central sanctuary were sustained by gifts from the people (Deut 14:28–29). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-18-commentary)

**v. 2:** “Although they have no inheritance among their brothers, the LORD is their inheritance, as He promised them.”

Guzik comments that God calls some among His people to focus on Him and His service; they may have less in tangible assets and material security, but the LORD Himself is their inheritance. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

Matthew Henry observes: “Care is taken that the priests entangle not themselves with the affairs of this life, nor enrich themselves with the wealth of this world; they have better things to mind.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/deuteronomy/18.htm)

---

## vv. 3–5 — The Priests’ Share of Sacrifices and Firstfruits

**v. 3:** “This shall be the priests’ share from the people who offer a sacrifice, whether a bull or a sheep: the priests are to be given the shoulder, the jowls, and the stomach.”

Guzik explains that from a typical sacrifice, the priests received the shoulder (front leg), the cheeks (jowls), and the stomach. The rest was either burnt before the LORD or returned to the offerer for a fellowship meal. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that these were regarded as the choice parts and were given to the priests *in addition to* the wave breast and heave leg of the peace offerings (Leviticus 7:32ff). Keil (cited by Pulpit) suggests these additional dues compensated for the falling off of income after the repeal of the law requiring every animal slaughtered to be a sacrifice at the sanctuary (Deut 12:15ff). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-18.html)

Precept Austin adds the practical note that the stomach (the rough stomach of ruminants) was used to make cheese — the lining was processed into a yellowish powder for curdling milk. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-18-commentary)

**v. 4:** “You are to give them the firstfruits of your grain, new wine, and oil, and the first wool sheared from your flock.”

Guzik notes that the first fleece of the sheep is mentioned only here in the Old Testament (citing Thompson). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

The Pulpit Commentary says this first-fleece prescription was an addition to the firstfruits already prescribed in Numbers 18:12–13. All these, though legally prescribed, were “free gifts on the part of the people; the neglect of the prescription incurred only moral blame, not judicial penalty.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-18.html)

Gill’s Exposition identifies the grain, wine, and oil offering as the *terumah* (heave offering), the measure of which was fixed by Jewish tradition (Exodus 22:29). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/18.htm)

**v. 5:** “For the LORD your God has chosen Levi and his sons out of all your tribes to stand and minister in His name for all time.”

The Pulpit Commentary notes the priesthood is established “in the family of Aaron” — “him and his sons forever” refers to the Aaronic line. To minister “in the Name of Jehovah” means not only by His appointment but with full power to act as mediator between the people and God. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-18.html)

---

## vv. 6–8 — The Country Levite Serving at the Central Sanctuary

**v. 6:** “Now if a Levite moves from any town of residence throughout Israel and comes in all earnestness to the place the LORD will choose…”

Guzik explains that Levites were distributed throughout Israel’s towns, but if one felt called to serve at the tabernacle/temple itself, he had the right to do so. G. Campbell Morgan is cited: “Special provision was now made for any priest whose heart prompted him to special service.” F.B. Meyer adds: “It is a blessed thing to feel an impulse like this… be true to it, nurse it, reverence it, thank God for it, trust and follow it where it leads.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

**v. 7:** “then he shall serve in the name of the LORD his God like all his fellow Levites who stand there before the LORD.”

The Levite who came with “all the desire of his mind” (v. 6, NKJV rendering) was allowed to minister alongside those already serving at the sanctuary.

**v. 8:** “They shall eat equal portions, even though he has received money from the sale of his father’s estate.”

Guzik notes that ideally the Levite from far away would receive the same amount from tithes and offerings as those stationed at the sanctuary. The phrase “besides what comes from the sale of his inheritance” means the Levite might have private means from selling family property — but that did not reduce his share. Clarke (cited by Guzik) observes that though Levites had no tribal land allotment, they could purchase houses, goods, and cattle, and even fields (1 Kings 2:26; Jeremiah 32:7–8). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

Gill adds that the equal portions included the skins and flesh of sin offerings, and perhaps even the daily sacrifices — “hence we learn, says Jarchi, that they divided the skins and flesh of the sin offerings.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/deuteronomy-18.html)

---

## vv. 9–11 — Prohibition of Occult Practices

**v. 9:** “When you enter the land that the LORD your God is giving you, do not imitate the detestable ways of the nations there.”

Guzik comments: “God knows that many people have a natural curiosity regarding the occult, and that curiosity often leads them to seek spiritually dangerous experiences.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

Matthew Henry notes the irony: “Was it possible that a people so blessed with Divine institutions, should ever be in any danger of making those their teachers whom God had made their captives?” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/deuteronomy/18.htm)

**v. 10:** “Let no one be found among you who sacrifices his son or daughter in the fire, practices divination or conjury, interprets omens, practices sorcery…”

The reference to children passing through fire points to Molech worship. Guzik notes the list that follows contains “eight offices or roles played by those given over to demonic and dark practices.” Maclaren (cited by Guzik) summarizes: “the first three refer to different means of reading the future, the next two to different means of influencing events, and the last three to different ways of consulting the dead.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

The Pulpit Commentary provides detailed Hebrew word studies on each term:

- **Divination** (קֶסֶם): cf. Ezekiel 21:21 where methods of divination are enumerated.
- **Observer of times** (מְעוֹנֵן): the Targum renders “observing hours”; LXX has “one who augurs”; some derive from עָנַן (cloud) meaning “interpreter of clouds,” others from עַיִן (eye) meaning one who cheats by optical fascinations.
- **Enchanter** (מְנַחֵשׁ): possibly ophiomancy (divination by serpents), though this is debated.
- **Witch** (מְכַשֵּׁף; LXX: φαρμακός): one who used drugs, herbs, and potions to produce magical effects. In Daniel 2:2 the Mecashephim appear alongside the Hartummim.
- **Charmer** (חֹבֵר חָבֶר): literally “one who binds,” i.e., a dealer in spells by tying knots, accompanied by incantation (Psalm 58:5). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-18.html)

**v. 11:** “…casts spells, consults a medium or spiritist, or inquires of the dead.”

The Pulpit Commentary explains:

- **Consulter with familiar spirits** (שֹׁאֵל אוֹב): one who inquires of an *Ob* or Python-spirit. This spirit was thought to dwell in the conjurer himself (Leviticus 20:27; 1 Samuel 28:7–8). The LXX renders ἐγγαστρίμυθοι (ventriloquists). The modern notion of a “familiar spirit” as an external spirit is “not known to Scripture.”
- **Wizard** (יִדְּעֹנִי): literally “the knowing one” — the English word “wizard” originally meant “the wise one” without evil connotation (Milton used it for the Magi).
- **Necromancer**: one who professed to call up the dead (cf. 1 Samuel 28:7). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-18.html)

Guzik applies this to the present day, warning that “whether a witch claims to be ‘white’ or ‘black,’ they still use occultic powers. This should be completely rejected by the people of God.” He adds that astrology, tarot cards, Ouija boards, and psychic hotlines all fall under these prohibitions. “Either the practitioners are greedy frauds (at best!), or worse, they gain their knowledge from satanic, demonic, spiritual sources.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

---

## vv. 12–14 — Why These Practices Are Forbidden

**v. 12:** “For whoever does these things is detestable to the LORD. And because of these detestable things, the LORD your God is driving out the nations before you.”

Guzik: “God’s judgment was upon the Canaanites because of these occult practices, and if Israel took up the same occult practices, they could also expect to receive the judgment of God.” He adds that the Canaanites were not only sex-worshippers (Ashtaroth) and money-worshippers (Baal), but their occult practices made them particularly ripe for judgment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

The Pulpit Commentary notes the connection between Molech-worship and magical arts in the text — not because Molech-worship was especially tied to soothsaying (an assertion “for which there is no evidence,” says Keil), but because idolatry and magic were intimately related, and Molech-worship was the form Israelites were most likely to encounter both in Moab and Canaan. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-18.html)

**v. 13:** “You must be blameless before the LORD your God.”

Guzik: “This was more than a general call to a holy life. This was a solemn warning to keep from any involvement with these detestable practices of the occult.” He references the Ephesian Christians who burned their occult books (Acts 19:19–20). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

The Pulpit Commentary notes the word translated “perfect” (תָּמִים) means “entire, whole” (Latin *integer*) and is rendered best as “upright” — the Israelites were to be sincere in relation to Jehovah. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-18.html)

**v. 14:** “Though these nations, which you will dispossess, listen to conjurers and diviners, the LORD your God has not permitted you to do so.”

Ellicott’s Commentary notes the Hebrew is more literally: “As for thee, not so hath Jehovah thy God given unto thee.” Rashi is cited: “He hath not left thee to hearken to observers of times and enchanters; for behold He hath given Shechinah to rest upon the prophets, and Urim and Thummim.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/18.htm)

---

## vv. 15–19 — The Promise of a Prophet Like Moses

This is the most theologically significant passage in the chapter and one where Protestant traditions share substantial agreement — all see it as ultimately fulfilled in Christ — though there are nuanced differences.

### The Traditional/Evangelical Reading (shared broadly)

**v. 15:** “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him.”

Guzik explains this Prophet is set in deliberate contrast to the dark occult practices just described. The Prophet would be “like Moses” — from among the people, a mediator, speaking God’s words. The NT repeatedly identifies Jesus as this Prophet: John 1:21, 25; 6:14; 7:40; Acts 3:22–23; 7:37. Guzik cites Spurgeon: “It would be a very interesting task for the young people to work out all the points in which Moses is a personal type of the Lord Jesus.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

Gill’s Exposition emphatically identifies this as the Messiah — not Joshua, Jeremiah, David, or a succession of prophets (contra Jarchi). “A single person is only spoken of; and there is a dissimilitude between Moses and anyone of the prophets, and all of them in succession (Deuteronomy 34:10), but the Messiah, with whom the whole agrees.” Gill notes that the Jews themselves expected a singular Prophet based on this passage (John 6:14). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/18.htm)

Matthew Henry is equally direct: “It is here promised concerning Christ, that there should come a Prophet, great above all the prophets… He is the Light of the world (John 8:12). He is the Word by whom God speaks to us (John 1:1; Hebrews 1:2)… This prophet is come, even JESUS; and is He that should come, and we are to look for no other.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/deuteronomy/18.htm)

**v. 16:** “This is what you asked of the LORD your God at Horeb on the day of the assembly, when you said, ‘Let us not hear the voice of the LORD our God or see this great fire anymore, so that we will not die!’”

Ellicott notes the profound significance that the Prophet like Moses was promised on “the day of the assembly” at Horeb when the law was given. “The Holy Spirit, who is Christ in us, was promised on the day of the delivery of the ‘letter that killeth.’” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/18.htm)

Guzik: At Sinai Israel begged for a mediator (Exodus 20:19–21). Like Moses, the coming Prophet would mediate — representing God to the people and the people before God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

**v. 17:** “Then the LORD said to me, ‘They have spoken well.’”

The people’s request for a mediator, rather than hearing God’s terrifying voice directly, was approved by God.

**v. 18:** “I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers. I will put My words in his mouth, and he will tell them everything I command him.”

Guzik: Like Moses, this Prophet would speak God’s word — not His own. Jesus said, “the words that I speak unto you I speak not of myself” (John 14:10, cited by Ellicott). Ellicott also connects this to the Holy Spirit: “He shall not speak of Himself. He shall receive of mine, and shall show it unto you” (John 16:13–14). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/18.htm)

Gill on “I will put My words in his mouth”: the doctrines of the Gospel come from God — words of truth, faith, righteousness, peace, pardon, life, and salvation. Christ declared these were not His own but the Father’s (John 7:16). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/18.htm)

**v. 19:** “And I will hold accountable anyone who does not listen to My words that the prophet speaks in My name.”

Guzik warns: “God would hold accountable (require) all those who rejected the Prophet.” He cites Spurgeon: “The day will come when he will require it of you in a much more violent sense than he does today; when you shall have passed beyond the region of mercy.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

Ellicott connects this to Hebrews 12:25: “For if they escaped not who refused Him that spake on earth, much more shall not we escape, if we turn away from Him that speaketh from heaven.” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/18.htm)

### Differences Among Protestant Traditions

**Reformed (Ligonier):** Ligonier emphasises that Jesus is not merely a prophet but the *Prophet-Mediator* — a special class to which only Moses and Jesus belong. “While this text predicts the rise of all the prophets in Israel, it also has a special messianic significance in pointing to a prophet who, like Moses, will also be the mediator of a covenant with God’s people… Unlike the other prophets, Moses and Jesus were figures through whom God established covenants and the attendant covenant stipulations, rituals, and processes for atonement.” Yet Jesus is far greater than Moses because He is the Son of God (Hebrews 3:1–6). (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/prophet-mediator)

**Pulpit Commentary (broader Anglican/evangelical):** The Pulpit Commentary presents a both-and view — the prophecy refers to the *prophetic succession* in Israel (the context of contrasting diviners with prophets, the need to discriminate true from false prophets, and the parallel with succession of priests, judges, and kings all point to a line of prophets). Yet at the same time, the use of the singular *nabhi* “suggests that the reference here may be to some individual in whom not only was the succession to culminate… It is to be concluded, then, that this promise has reference ultimately to the Messiah, the Great Revealer of God, between whom and Moses there should be a long succession of prophets.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-18.html)

**Coffman’s Commentary (conservative Church of Christ):** Coffman strongly rejects the “succession of prophets” view as “ridiculous,” citing Deuteronomy 34:10 (“there hath not arisen a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses”) and the 500-year prophetic silence between the Testaments. He insists the prophecy applies solely and uniquely to Christ and lists numerous parallels between Moses and Jesus. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/deuteronomy-18.html)

---

## v. 20 — The Penalty for a False Prophet

“But if any prophet dares to speak a message in My name that I have not commanded him to speak, or to speak in the name of other gods, that prophet must be put to death.”

Guzik distinguishes two categories: (a) speaking presumptuously in God’s name — claiming to speak for God when God has not sent him, and (b) speaking in the name of false gods. Both carry the death penalty in ancient Israel. He notes Merrill’s observation: “Of the three major institutions of ancient Israelite social and religious life — royalty, the priesthood, and prophetism — only the last was charismatic and nonsuccessive.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

Ellicott references Rashi, who illustrates with the case of Hananiah (Jeremiah 28): Hananiah prophesied that Jeconiah would return from Babylon within two years; Jeremiah declared he would die that year, and he died within two months. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/18.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary adds that a false prophet speaking in the name of other gods “was himself to be treated as a blasphemer, and to be put to death.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-18.html)

---

## vv. 21–22 — How to Test a Prophet

**v. 21:** “You may ask in your heart, ‘How can we recognize a message that the LORD has not spoken?’”

Guzik notes: it was easy to identify a prophet who spoke in the name of Baal. The harder case was someone speaking *in the LORD’s name* but presumptuously. How to tell? (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

**v. 22:** “When a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD and the message does not come to pass or come true, that is a message the LORD has not spoken. The prophet has spoken presumptuously. Do not be afraid of him.”

Guzik explains this is the test of **predictive accuracy**. If the predicted event does not happen, the prophet is false. However, Guzik adds that this is not the *only* test. Deuteronomy 13:1–5 provides another: even if a prophet performs a sign or wonder that comes to pass, if he leads people to follow other gods, he must be rejected and put to death. “Whether a predicted thing happened or not was one test of a prophet, but not the only test. It was the first test, not the final test” (citing Kalland). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)

The Pulpit Commentary clarifies: “The reference here is to the prediction of proximate events — events that were to happen within a limited period, but which were not such as one not divinely instructed could foresee.” This was “a more certain test than such as was offered by signs and wonders (Deuteronomy 13:2).” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/deuteronomy-18.html)

Gill notes that this test does not apply when a condition is “either expressed or implied, as the repentance or disobedience of a people; see Jeremiah 18:7.” A conditional prophecy (e.g., Jonah’s pronouncement over Nineveh) that does not come to pass because of repentance does not make the prophet false. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/18.htm)

Ellicott adds that “this is one form of our Lord’s test for all prophets, ‘By their fruits (i.e., the results of their teaching, not its first impressions) ye shall know them.’” (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/18.htm)

Guzik concludes on the final phrase “Do not be afraid of him”: “Genuine prophets were to be treated with respect… False prophets could be disregarded. At best, such false prophets spoke from themselves (presumptuously). At worst, they were instruments of demonic deception (as in Deuteronomy 18:9–11).” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-18/)
